findings.claim: "In 1890, the new Kaiser dismissed Bismarck. Wilhelm II was twenty-nine, ambitious and determined to be his own Chancellor."
findings.truth: Wilhelm II was born on 27 January 1859 and dismissed Bismarck in March 1890, so he was 31. He was 29 when he became Kaiser in June 1888.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Wilhelm II, German Emperor' (birth 27 January 1859; Bismarck dismissed March 1890)

findings.claim: Card 9: q "By 1912, the SPD had become the ____ party in the Reichstag." / a "Largest."
findings.truth: A one-word answer needs a substantive question and a fuller answer. Rewritten as "Which party was the largest in the Reichstag after the 1912 election?" with the SPD, 110 seats and over a third of the vote.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief; 1912 result already stated in the lesson

findings.claim: Card 11: q "By 1914, Germany's population had risen from 49 million in 1890 to roughly ____." / a "68 million."
findings.truth: The question gives the answer away and the answer is one figure. Rewritten as a substantive question with both figures in the answer.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: The Prussian three-class franchise "gave the wealthiest men votes worth seventeen times those of the poorest" (repeated in flashcard 12).
findings.truth: The three-class system split taxpayers into three bands each choosing a third of the electors. Weightings quoted in the literature vary from about 17 to about 20 times, and the figure could not be pinned to a source. Left as written.
findings.evidence: no source found within this session's fetch budget

findings.claim: "Examiners want the domestic angle on the Navy Laws..."
findings.truth: An invented exam claim. The spec bullet does name "the domestic importance of the Navy Laws", so the point is made from the specification instead.
findings.evidence: spec, Part one: Germany and the growth of democracy

findings.claim: "By 1912 the navy was costing the equivalent of around half the entire imperial budget" (repeated in flashcard 5 and practice question 3).
findings.truth: Probably too high. Naval estimates in 1913 were roughly 450-470 million marks against Reich expenditure of well over 2 billion; the armed forces together, not the navy alone, took the large share. No figure could be confirmed, so left as written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anglo-German naval arms race' gives no budget share

findings.claim: "The Kaiser called them 'a gang of traitors'."
findings.truth: This direct quotation could not be sourced. Wilhelm II's documented jibe at the Social Democrats is "vaterlandslose Gesellen" (fellows without a fatherland). Recommend de-quoting to "denounced them as unpatriotic" if Tom agrees.
findings.evidence: no source found for the quoted wording

findings.claim: "Within forty-eight hours the SPD's Friedrich Ebert had signed the armistice on 11 November 1918."
findings.truth: Matthias Erzberger of the Centre Party signed the armistice at Compiegne. Ebert became Chancellor on 9 November and never signed it. Lesson 4 of this same unit correctly names Erzberger as the signatory.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 4; Wikipedia 'Armistice of 11 November 1918'

findings.claim: "The same day the Kaiser fled across the border into the neutral Netherlands"; mark scheme: "Hindenburg told the Kaiser the troops would not fight for him; Wilhelm fled to Holland on 9 November 1918."
findings.truth: Wilhelm left Spa and crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November 1918, the day after the abdication was announced. It was Wilhelm Groener, not Hindenburg, who told the Kaiser the army would no longer stand behind him, with Hindenburg present.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Abdication of Wilhelm II' - "On 10 November, Wilhelm left for exile in the Netherlands"

findings.claim: The Kiel mutiny dated "late October 1918" in the body, the match set, the mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The order to sail was issued in late October and sailors refused at Wilhelmshaven on 30-31 October, but the Kiel mutiny itself began on 3 November 1918.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kiel mutiny' - began 3 November 1918

findings.claim: "In late October a new civilian government under Prince Max of Baden took office."
findings.truth: Prince Max of Baden was appointed Chancellor on 3 October 1918, early in the month.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Maximilian of Baden'; standard chronology of the October reforms

findings.claim: "From the USPD's far-left fringe came the Spartacus League, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg."
findings.truth: The Spartacus group formed during the war (1915-16) and then operated as the far-left wing inside the USPD from 1917; it did not emerge out of the USPD. The wording is a common textbook shortcut and was left alone.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Spartakusgruppe

findings.claim: "Germany lost ... the Saar coalfield to Allied control."
findings.truth: The Saar was placed under League of Nations administration for fifteen years, with the coal mines handed to France. It was not simply Allied control.
findings.evidence: Treaty of Versailles, Articles 45-50

findings.claim: "The occupation lasted until late 1923."
findings.truth: Passive resistance was called off in September 1923, but French and Belgian troops stayed in the Ruhr until 1925; the last French troops left Duisburg on 25 August 1925.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Occupation of the Ruhr' - last French troops evacuated 25 August 1925

findings.claim: "Hyperinflation did not hurt all Germans equally - this nuance is what examiners want to see."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; removed, keeping the historical point.
findings.evidence: checker brief: invented exam claims are removed

findings.claim: "Examiners punish students who claim hyperinflation hurt all Germans equally."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; rewritten as a direct instruction to the student.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: Reparations "132 billion gold marks, payable over 42 years" (repeated in the collapsible as "spread across forty-two years").
findings.truth: The 1921 London Schedule set 132 billion gold marks but the repayment period is stated differently in different sources; 42 years could not be confirmed. Left as written.
findings.evidence: no source found within this session's fetch budget

findings.claim: "Examiners regularly flag that students confuse these uprisings..."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; rewritten as "Students often confuse these uprisings".
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "The constitution had two structural weaknesses that examiners want students to spot."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; removed.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "the same German judiciary that hanged left-wing rebels gave right-wing rebels suspended sentences"; mark scheme: "the rapid execution of Spartacist leaders the year before".
findings.truth: Weimar courts did not hang left-wing rebels. Liebknecht and Luxemburg were murdered by Freikorps without any trial on 15 January 1919, as the lesson itself says two paragraphs earlier. Judicial death sentences on the left (for example Eugen Levine after the Bavarian Soviet Republic) were carried out by firing squad.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own account of 15 January 1919

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag that students confuse the Spartacist uprising ... every series."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; rewritten without the examiner-report assertion.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "a fiasco that arrested Hitler within hours, but his five-month trial turned him from a regional agitator into a national figure"; the same "within hours" appears in a practice interpretation.
findings.truth: Hitler was arrested on 11 November 1923, two days after the march, which the lesson body states correctly. The trial ran from 26 February to 1 April 1924, about five weeks, not five months.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson body; standard trial dates

findings.claim: "Between 1919 and 1933 Germany had twenty-one different cabinets, averaging seven months each."
findings.truth: Twenty-one cabinets across about fourteen years averages roughly eight months. The flashcard version ("21 cabinets in 14 years") is fine. Too small to be worth an edit.
findings.evidence: arithmetic

findings.claim: "he and General Erich Ludendorff burst into a beer hall where ... Gustav von Kahr was speaking".
findings.truth: Hitler burst in with SA men; Ludendorff was fetched and arrived about an hour later. A common textbook compression, left alone.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of 8 November 1923

findings.claim: "The German historian Detlev Peukert argued Weimar was 'dancing on a volcano'."
findings.truth: The quotation cannot be sourced to Peukert, whose Weimar book (Die Weimarer Republik, 1987) argues the republic was a "crisis of classical modernity". "Dancing on a volcano" is a period catchphrase, not a Peukert coinage. His argument is kept; the quotation is dropped.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Detlev Peukert'

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag this confusion every series." (Dawes vs Young)
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; rewritten.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: Germany signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact "alongside fifteen other major powers".
findings.truth: There were fifteen original signatories in total on 27 August 1928, Germany among them, so fourteen others.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kellogg-Briand Pact' - fifteen signatories listed

findings.claim: "the first synchronised-sound film The Blue Angel (1930)".
findings.truth: The Blue Angel was not the first synchronised-sound film; The Jazz Singer (1927) came first. It is usually described as the first major German sound film. The unverifiable superlative is removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'The Blue Angel'

findings.claim: Ebert "was replaced by 78-year-old Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg".
findings.truth: Hindenburg was born on 2 October 1847. He was 77 when elected in April 1925 and took office in May 1925; he turned 78 that October.
findings.evidence: Hindenburg's birth date, 2 October 1847

findings.claim: "In October 1925 he signed the Locarno Treaties" (repeated in the exam tip, match set and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The treaties were negotiated and initialled at Locarno on 16 October 1925 but formally signed in London on 1 December 1925. October is the usual textbook shorthand and the year is right; changing it would ripple through five fields for little gain.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Locarno Treaties

findings.claim: "the Young Plan of 1929, named after another American banker (Owen Young)".
findings.truth: Owen D. Young was an American lawyer and industrialist, chairman of General Electric, not a banker. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Owen D. Young'

findings.claim: "In May 1928, three months before the Wall Street Crash..."
findings.truth: The May 1928 election was seventeen months before the crash of October 1929.
findings.evidence: arithmetic; the lesson dates both events correctly elsewhere

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag this every series: it was the Depression that caused Hitler's rise..."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; the historical point is kept.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "Five separate emergency decrees passed in 1931 alone."
findings.truth: Five is the 1930 figure. The standard Weimar table (which the lesson itself uses two sentences later for 1932: 66 decrees against 5 Reichstag laws) records 5 decrees in 1930 and a much larger number in 1931. The sentence is rewritten to name 1930 without asserting a 1931 number.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own 1932 figures come from the same table

findings.claim: "The Communists (KPD) also doubled their vote, reaching 13.1%"; mark scheme: "the Communist KPD also doubled".
findings.truth: The KPD went from 10.6% in 1928 to 13.1% in 1930 - a rise of about a quarter, not a doubling. The lesson's own key fact gives 10.6% to 16.9% by November 1932.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's key fact

findings.claim: "a thirteenfold rise in four years" (12 to 230 seats) and "the Nazi vote had grown thirteenfold in four years".
findings.truth: 12 seats to 230 seats is a nineteenfold rise; 2.6% to 37.4% of the vote is a fourteenfold rise. Thirteenfold is wrong on either measure.
findings.evidence: arithmetic on the lesson's own figures

findings.claim: "Two examiner trip-wires for this lesson" and "Direction of causation matters and gets flagged every series."
findings.truth: Invented exam claims; removed.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "a party that had just lost 34 Reichstag seats in November came to power eight weeks later".
findings.truth: 6 November 1932 to 30 January 1933 is about twelve weeks.
findings.evidence: arithmetic on the lesson's own dates

findings.claim: "Papen's cabinet was nicknamed the 'Cabinet of Barons' because nine of its eleven members were aristocrats."
findings.truth: The Papen cabinet had about ten posts, of which roughly six or seven went to nobles. The precise ratio is stated differently in different sources, so the sentence is generalised rather than given a new number.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Papen cabinet' - nine core ministerial posts, six nobles and three commoners

findings.claim: "By 1936 unemployment was down to one million", repeated in the key fact ("six million in 1933 to one million by 1936") and in the revision tip, which asks students to memorise the 1933, 1936 and 1939 figures.
findings.truth: The standard German series gives an annual average of about 1.6 million for 1936 and about 0.9 million for 1937, so one million belongs to 1937 rather than 1936. The low monthly point of 1936 was close to a million, so the sentence is defensible on one reading. No online source could be reached to settle it, and it needs Tom's textbook table. Options: (a) change both to "1.6 million by 1936", (b) change both to "under a million by 1937", (c) leave.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Economy of Nazi Germany' gives no year-by-year figures
findings.ruling: Option (a)+(b): 1.6 million by 1936, under a million by 1937; prose and key fact aligned.

findings.claim: Final key-fact revision tip: "write down four key dates ... 1933, 1934, 1935 (Mother's Cross), 1936 (HJ Law)".
findings.truth: The lesson correctly dates the Mother's Cross to 1938 in two places. The revision tip contradicted it and would have taught a wrong date.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson body and key fact

findings.claim: "resistance from the churches and the white-flight of older youth".
findings.truth: "White flight" describes racial residential movement in US history. It is the wrong term here; the point is that older teenagers drifted away from the Hitler Youth.
findings.evidence: term misuse

findings.claim: The Confessional Church "formed in 1934 under Niemoller and Bonhoeffer's Barmen Declaration".
findings.truth: The Barmen Declaration was drafted by Karl Barth with Hans Asmussen at the Barmen synod of May 1934. Bonhoeffer was in London and was not one of its authors, though he was a leading Confessing Church figure.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the Barmen synod, 29-31 May 1934

findings.claim: "PE rose to fifteen periods a week to build soldiers and mothers"; mark scheme: "PE up to 15 periods".
findings.truth: Fifteen periods a week is three PE lessons every day, which is not credible. The number almost certainly comes from the standard textbook claim that PE took about 15 per cent of school time. Recommend changing both to "around 15 per cent of school time", but the source figure needs Tom's confirmation before the number is altered.
findings.evidence: implausibility of the stated figure; the common 15% formulation
findings.ruling: Around 15 per cent of school time, prose and mark scheme.

findings.claim: "By 1938 around half of Germany's 500,000 Jews had emigrated."
findings.truth: About 282,000 of the 523,000 Jews living in Germany in January 1933 had emigrated by September 1939, roughly half. By the end of 1938 the cumulative figure was nearer thirty per cent; the surge followed Kristallnacht.
findings.evidence: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'German Jewish Refugees, 1933-1939'

findings.claim: "Nazi sociologists called this the 'atomisation' of public life."
findings.truth: "Atomisation" is an analytical term used by later historians and social theorists of totalitarianism, not a Nazi coinage or a Nazi-era description of their own policy.
findings.evidence: term attribution

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag the conflation regularly." (SS / SA / Gestapo)
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; rewritten.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "It also asks the question that examiners reward most in 12-mark essays..."
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; the question itself is kept.
findings.evidence: checker brief

findings.claim: "The fifth leaflet was smuggled out of Germany and dropped over the country by Allied aircraft"; the same claim appears in a mark scheme.
findings.truth: It was the sixth and final leaflet. Helmuth James von Moltke smuggled the text out through Scandinavia to Britain, and it was air-dropped over Germany in 1943 retitled 'The Manifesto of the Students of Munich'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'White Rose'

findings.claim: "Stauffenberg, General Ludwig Beck and three others were arrested and shot in the courtyard of the Bendlerblock that night."
findings.truth: Four men were shot in the courtyard (Stauffenberg, Olbricht, Mertz von Quirnheim and Haeften). Beck was allowed to attempt suicide inside the building, failed twice and was finished off by a sergeant. He did die that night by gunshot, so the sentence is loose rather than false.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of 20-21 July 1944

findings.claim: "Around 5,000 people connected to the plot or its sympathisers were eventually arrested", alongside "around 200 conspirators were executed".
findings.truth: The usual pairing in the literature is about 7,000 arrested and about 4,980 executed in the wider Gestapo sweep. The lesson's 5,000 looks like the execution figure used as an arrest figure, but sources vary by scope, so it was left alone.
findings.evidence: sources vary; no single authority checked within budget

findings.claim: "Around 6,000 people attended a Swing festival in Hamburg in 1940."
findings.truth: Scholarly accounts of the February 1940 Hamburg swing festival give 500-600 attendees, though 6,000 appears in some UK textbooks. Left as written because it matches the textbook tradition this unit follows.
findings.evidence: Peukert's account of the Hamburg swing scene gives the lower figure

summary: Fourteen lessons checked against the AQA 8145 spec and its assessment section; exam-format claims (Paper 1 Section A question types, 4/4/8/4/8/12 marks) are accurate throughout, and no spec-scope breaches were found. 52 edits fix twelve invented examiner claims, two HIGH errors (Ebert credited with signing the armistice; Weimar courts said to have hanged left-wing rebels), a cluster of wrong dates and figures (Kiel mutiny, Prince Max's appointment, the Kaiser's flight, the Ruhr occupation's end, the sixth White Rose leaflet, the 1930 emergency-decree count, KPD 'doubling', 'thirteenfold', Hindenburg's age, the Mother's Cross revision tip) and two unsourced attributions (Peukert's 'dancing on a volcano', the Barmen Declaration).
